# **ON THE EVOLUTION OF ALL THINGS COGNITIVE**

### 

### **B. Brian Kuhlman, MS**

### **Department of Educational Psychology, University of Utah**

What follows is a scientifically palatable explanation of all things cognitive. The major topics of this paper include: sensorimotor coordination, (non)associative learning, motivation, consciousness, working memory, executive functions, metacognition, episodic / prospective memory, and abstract / symbolic thought. While demonstrating some novelty, the discussion draws heavily on recent publications from the fields of information science, evolutionary ecology, cognitive psychology, and biological anthropology. 

The paper is organized as follows:  
  [1\. NATURAL HABITS](#1.-natural-habits), in which a humble framework for grand consilience is presented.  
  [2\. COGNITIVE BIOLOGY](#2.-cognitive-biology), in which the basics of cognition are juxtaposed.  
  [3\. BUZZING MATERIAL](#3.-buzzing-material), in which the evolutionary roots of consciousness are postulated.  
  [4\. ANIMAL VOLITION](#4.-animal-volition), in which cognition’s hierarchy and modularity habits are coordinated.   
  [5\. INTELLIGENT CREATURES](#5.-intelligent-creatures), in which the state of the future is considered.

## 

## 

## **1\. NATURAL HABITS**  {#1.-natural-habits}

Organisms are kept alive via the hierarchical coordination of habits. Metabolism, the most fundamental cellular habit, is itself a coordination of molecular-level habits (e.g., assembly and disassembly). Further, morphodynamic habits like protein formation are coordinations of atomic-level habits (e.g., energy use and release), and thermodynamic habits like entropy are coordinations of quantum-level habits (e.g., wave-particle duality). In other words, life is a hierarchical coordination of habits; or, it’s habits *all the way down*.

The academic study of habit coordination is called information science. Theories in this domain posit that any real object (e.g., the entire universe) is a hierarchical coordination of habits. That is, anything observable (any bit of information) is, by definition, habitual. Stated more directly, all objects of nature exist *because* they coordinate the habits of their constituent parts. If nature ceased the coordination of habits, entropy would take over and the universe would be drained of all information. 

Information science is operating at the bleeding edge of academic consilience efforts and, while it is beyond the scope of this paper to explicate theoretical foundations of information science, the interested reader will find that excellent introductions have recently been published (e.g., see Auletta’s (2012) *Cognitive Biology* and Deacon’s (2011) *Incomplete Nature*). The important point here is that information science provides a scientific framework for consilience between historically siloed academic domains such as physiology, ecology and psychology. 

Darwinian evolutionary theory is compatible with information theory. Adaptation, a concept from evolutionary theory, is foundational in the approach to cognition that our discussion will take. In informational terms, adaptation is the coordination of organismal habits (e.g., reproduction) with ecological habits (e.g., natural selection). For example, plant vernalization--the acquisition of flowering ability over a Winter season--is adaptive because it coordinates the timing of a plant’s germination habit with the timing of pollinator habits. Because of vernalization, flowering happens in the warm Spring season which is also when pollinating insects are active. In evolutionary terms, a habit is adaptive if it preserves a phenotype. So, in post hoc analysis, vernalization is deemed adaptive because it fosters the continuation of a genetic line. As a concept, adaptation is synonymous with Darwinian success. Historically, the study of adaptive habits laid the groundwork for the biological philosophy known as functionalism. 

The next section discusses what functionalists describe as “cognitive” adaptations, coordinations and habits.

## **2\. COGNITIVE BIOLOGY** {#2.-cognitive-biology}

Functionalists typically organize adaptations along a continuum of complexity that runs from lower-order (e.g., cellular metabolism) to higher-order (e.g., human language). However, recent efforts have used a more categorical organization. In his dissertation, Duijn (2011) postulates a categorical distinction between *phenotypic plasticity*, the ability of an organism to change its phenotype in response to ecological changes, and *sensorimotor coordination*. He claims that cognition is the coordination of sensory and motor habits. Categorically, then, cognition is a subset of motility adaptations. Sessile organisms like plants and fungi do exhibit phenotypic plasticity but, because they do not move around, they do not exhibit cognition. Thus, while it is clear that plants, slime and fungi exhibit sophisticated adaptations, they cannot be categorized as cognitive or intelligent creatures. 

Cognitive biology emerged from motile biology, and cognition has always been constrained by morphology. For example, the earliest neural networks were not cephalized (centralized in a brain). Likely, cephalization evolved as a result of the bilateral body plan which has a clear anterior (mouth) and posterior (anus) end. Bilateral sensorimotor coordination typically involves forward, or anterior-leading, movements. As Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007b) write (p.234):   
Once a single, forward direction of locomotion was deﬁned, the anterior parts of animals became the ﬁrst to meet or seek various stimuli in the environment. This resulted in the concentration of sensory cells in the front end of the animal—its head—and of other neural elements along the body. Such differentiation between sensory and motor regions allowed integration of sensory inputs and coordination of motor outputs within regions as well as coordinated interactions between regions.

Claiming that the brain evolved to coordinate histological habits of motile organisms complements Duijn’s postulation that cognition *is* sensorimotor coordination. Describing early metazoan sensorimotor coordination, Christensen (2007) provides a helpful framework that is summarized by Duijn (2011) as follows (p.81):  
The first level of cognitive control in Metazoa (animals) is provided by ‘central pattern generators’ (CPGs). CPGs are control systems responsible for the generation and regulation of stable behavioral patterns by generating rhythmic contractions across a bodily surface. CPGs are composed of premotor interneurons, which generate oscillations, coupled to motoneurons which stimulate the muscles to generate rhythmic patterns... Feedback control over multi-stable behavioral patterns through CPGs characterizes the sensorimotor behaviors of many Metazoa, such as the lamprey, the worm *C. Elegans*, and cnidarians such as hydra and jellyfish. 

Controversially, Duijn (2011) claims that the animal kingdom does *not* have a monopoly on cognitive adaptations. Bi-stable sensorimotor coordination, which Duijn labels “minimal cognition,” has been documented in the chemotactic behavior of motile single-celled organisms like *E. Coli*. He explains (p.80):  
Due to the rate-difference between the fast-paced two-component signaling (positive feedback) pathway and the much slower methylation (negative feedback) pathway, the bacterium is able to compare the current state of affairs with that of previous ones so that it can modulate its behavior accordingly. The chemotaxis module regulates the bacterium’s action-selection by modulating its relative propensity to run or to tumble. Behavioral switching is based on contextual factors which facilitates the sensorimotor coordination of the bacterium. Cognitive control over behavioral bi-stability provides these organisms with an extension of basic homeostatic processes, enabling them to optimize the external conditions for their metabolism by navigating to niches that best support growth and survival. 

Functionally, sensorimotor coordination is an adaptive habit of locomotion; cognitive control enables the organism to discover better places. Duijn (2011) points out that motile micro-organisms reuse the sensorimotor coordination habit, or module, in a number of interesting ways such as phototaxis (light), aerotaxis (oxygen), thermotaxis (temperature), and gravitotaxis (gravity). Clearly, *E. Coli* are more sophisticated than their cell count suggests. And by referring to these adaptations as examples of *minimal* cognition, Duijn smooths the stretch of imagination required by his ideas. Nevertheless, his work is controversial. 

Disregarding the distinction between motile and sessile adaptations, Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) focus instead on the distinction between associative and nonassociative learning habits. Nonassociative learning habits, which include habituation and sensitization, coordinate the gradual change of a response to repeated stimulus presentations. Habituation involves a decrease, and sensitization involves an increase, in response magnitude across time. While admitting that plants like *Mimosa* and protozoa like *E. Coli* exhibit nonassociative learning, Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) maintain that the animal kingdom, metazoa, are the only class of organisms that exhibit associative learning and, thus, enjoy an effective monopoly on cognitive adaptations. 

In animals, the functional timespan of these habits can be either short- or long-term. Short-term nonassociative learning habits are mediated by transient neurotransmitter reaction cascades. For example, serotonin initiates the cascade of reactions that coordinate the sensitization of the *Aplysia* gill withdrawal reflex (Klein, Camardo & Kandel, 1982). Long-term nonassociative learning habits require two factors: synaptic plasticity and epigenetic changes. Synaptic plasticity involves the growth of new synaptic connections (Bailey, Bartsch & Kandel, 1996\) and the persistence of structural changes at the synapse (Hawkins, Kandel & Bailey, 2006). Epigenetic changes like DNA methylation and histone acetylation are also known to be involved in the coordination of long-term nonassociative learning habits (Levenson & Sweatt, 2005). 

Nonassociative learning habits modulate the magnitude of an organism’s “innate” reflexes; they either heighten or dampen dispositions. In contrast, associative learning functions within the organism’s lifespan by creating new and extinguishing old reflexes. More specifically, classical and instrumental conditioning mechanisms coordinate new associations between stimuli (as in the coupling of unconditioned and conditioned stimuli) or between stimuli and responses (as in the reinforcement of an operant behavior). Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a; 2007b; 2010\) claim that, by definition, cognition *is* the coordination of associative learning habits. 

There is a good basis for this animal-centric claim. Ginsberg and Jablonka point out that neural networks provide the only known substrate of associative learning habits. They write (2007a; p.222):   
Some of the molecular machinery that enables learning in protozoa and plants (e.g., ion channels and second messengers) is the same as that seen in animals with a nervous system, but in spite of the biochemical similarities, learning by neural animals is fundamentally different. It occurs in an interconnected system of cells specialized for communication. Neurons are always part of a neural system—at its simplest, a diffuse nerve net—which depends on the structural and functional properties of the neuron: its elongated ﬁbers, which allow it to link spatially remote cells, and the chemical and electrical signals propagated via these ﬁbers. Together, these features enable precise and rapid communication between speciﬁc cells. *…* The neural network structure allowed speciﬁc types of learning and memory, which are observed in the simplest extant neural animals, the cnidarians and the ctenophores.

Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) outline a list of five preconditions for associative learning, which includes (i) an interconnected nervous system, (ii) nonassociative learning habits (habituation and sensitization) that can modulate reﬂex behavior; (iii) sensorimotor coordination and integration of information coming from multiple sensors; (iv) synaptic plasticity; and (v) some centralization of the nervous system, aka encephalization. 

Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) clarify that the coordination of associative learning is enabled by Hebbian learning and reentrant signaling. Hebb’s (1949) postulate is a simple rule that governs neural coordination and constrains synaptic plasticity; it is the principle that neurons who fire together, wire together. In line with the Hebbian rule, simple models for neural classical conditioning assume that sensory pathways for conditioned and unconditioned stimuli must converge anatomically. While synaptic plasticity is necessary it is also insufficient to explain associative learning (see Martin, Grimwood & Morris, 2000). Reentrant signaling--the reciprocal, forward and backward, transmission of signals between neural modules--is another crucial factor. Edelman and Tononi (2000) argue that reentrant networks make the signaling between nerve groups more persistent which reduces entropy in, or clarifies, the signal. This enables ﬁner and more reliable relations between speciﬁc stimuli and responses. So, associative learning is the coordination of “Hebbian” and reentrant signalling habits. 

In summary, Ginsberg and Jablonka make a compelling case that associative learning coevolved with the brain. The animal brain is organized as a hierarchical and reentrant network of “small-worlds” or processing modules. According to a confluence of research findings, this type of (hierarchical, reentrant, and modular) organization reflects both the structural and functional nature of brain circuitry (Sporns, 2011). In a later section of this paper, I will argue that Ginsberg and Jablonka’s (2007a; 2007b; 2010\) work is compatible with Duijn’s (2011) model when considered in the light of how the brain employs “higher-order” cognitive control. But first, let us consider a scientifically palatable explanation of motivation and consciousness.

## 

## **3\. BUZZING MATERIAL** {#3.-buzzing-material}

Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) posit that the roots of consciousness grew from the epiphenomenal buzz of sensorimotor coordination. They write (p.220):  
The unavoidable consequence of all the sensations that result from the incessant and persistent neural stimulation of the animal’s external and internal sensors is a global byproduct of neural activity we call “overall sensation.” We suggest, by way of metaphor, that it is a kind of “white-noise sensation”—a weak, completely functionless, and meaningless side-effect of an interconnected sensory-motor system, which is dynamically processing electrical and chemical signals triggered by sensors, communicated to effectors, sent back to sensors again, and so on.

The white noise or buzzing sensation is a side-effect of reentrant signaling; it is epiphenomenal. They go on to explain that the buzz is not a proper feeling or experience but is rather more like the raw ‘material’ of experience. 

Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) go on to distinguish between *limited* and *unlimited* experiencing. They write (p.221):  
“Limited experiencing” occurs when an animal has several types of overall sensations that follow body changes triggered by sensory stimulation, and when such overall sensations become integrated and persist. ... Each overall sensation has a different pattern of global activity. An animal with such sensory states has inner feelings, but these are not motivational states. 

Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a) claim that the crucial turning point--the emergence of basic consciousness on Earth--happens when Metazoan neural networks begin to coordinate epiphenomenal feelings with nonassociative learning mechanisms. They write (p.221):  
\[Prior to the emergence of consciousness,\] experiencing is limited both because it is based on a limited learning ability, which can only modulate pre-existing reﬂexes, and because the inner feelings do not yet have a function, so evolution based on them is limited. A system can be deﬁned as one with “unlimited experiencing” when a theoretically very large number of whole-organism sensory states can be generated, and when these states can be given a value and function as motivational states. 

In other words, consciousness is synonymous with motivation and it co-evolved with associative learning. Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007b) claim that, once experiences “can be given a value,” they have transformed from mere buzzing materials into *categorizing sensory states* (CSS). They write (p.236, italics are my own):  
During associative learning, new paths of exploration lead to an “attractor,” the dynamic end state at which the animal’s physiology “settles.” For example, a sensory state associated with a need for food initiates and then constrains and guides the \[animal’s\] exploration process toward the stabilized attractor state, satiation. A new learnt cue associated with the food that is found will have effects on the CSS and trigger its future activation. In other words, the animal learns that the cue is speciﬁcally predictive (in this case that it predicts food), so when encountered again, the CSS will guide the food-related behavior of the animal. *CSSs are therefore ﬂexible value systems: they are the neural dynamic structures that are necessary for the animal to modify its behavior according to the salience of a new cue.*

While the preceding passage employed terms from dynamical systems theory (e.g., attractors) the following passage captures the essence of CSSs in more functionalist terms:  
The function of CSSs is to evaluate inputs and generate outputs: the effects of an input (an external stimulus or the animal’s own actions) (1) are incorporated into a pre-existing CSS on the basis of the previous learning history of the animal and (2) generate actions by guiding selective stabilization processes, which maintain/reinforce or modify/reverse this CSS until an adaptive state is reached. (Ginsberg and Jablonka \[2007b\]; p.237)

CSSs, or conscious motivations, are the coordinators of associative learning. Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007b) claim that every CSS has a positive or negative quality. Along with the valence dimension, motivational states may be categorized along other dimensions such as arousal and granularity (Feldman Barrett & Bliss-Moreau, 2010). While a thorough review of motivation taxonomies is beyond the scope of this paper, it is noteworthy that all of the currently prominent models (e.g., Feldman Barrett, 2006; Panksepp, 2010\) agree with Ginsberg and Jablonka’s (2007b) claim that the valence of a CSS is what enables it to coordinate the “punishment” or “reward” of an organism’s behavior. In other words, while many animals may have “unlimited experiencing,” some buzzing materials (valence) are more memorable than others (arousal). 

By elucidating the role of experience in learning, Ginsberg and Jablonka (2007a; 2007b; 2010\) have successfully integrated the prevailing scientific explanations of behavior and consciousness. If presented a century earlier, these ideas might have given Pavlov, Skinner and Watson the buzz of vertigo. Yet this framework is undeniably compatible with behaviorist physiological findings, which makes it an exemplar of modern (neo-)functionalism. 

As productive as it is, the Ginsberg and Jablonka framework leaves a few unanswered questions. They have explained the roots of consciousness, but what about its stem and leaves? How can we make sense of phenomena like working memory, metacognition, episodic and prospective thinking? These are the topics of this paper’s next section which, you may be glad to know, contains a number of pictures. 

## **4\. ANIMAL VOLITION** {#4.-animal-volition}

*Scientific research is likely to result in a conservative naturalization of volition. Attention and memory provide relevant comparisons here: these are folk concepts that have gained a secure scientific footing as major scientific research fields. This research has revealed a great deal of structure not present in the folk concepts but it has not shown them to be basically wrong: attention really does involve selective focus, and memory really does involve retrieving information about the past. Plausibly, volition really does involve forming goals and controlling action in relation to intentions.*  
Christensen (2007, p.25)  
	  
Our discussion turns now to the topic of animal volition. While a philosophical treatise addressing free will, teleonomy and teleology is beyond the scope of this paper (see Auletta \[2012\], Deacon \[2011\], and Duijn \[2011\] for thorough discussions\], the following section will present a theoretical framework for the hierarchical coordination of cognition and action. To that end, I will summarize recent theories about the biological bases of working memory, metacognition, episodic memory and prospective thinking. In neuropsychological terms, this discussion is moving into the realm of executive functions. 

One of the explanatory difficulties in this domain is demonstrating the complementarity of distributed and localized brain functions. On the one hand, basic neurocognitive controls are undeniably distributed throughout areas of the brain, which argues for modular independence. On the other hand, neuropsychological researchers have compellingly demonstrated that the brain’s “association” circuits do, in fact, coordinate the habits of the brain’s “primary” circuits (for an excellent review, see Sporns \[2011\]). This is an argument for modular interdependence and hierarchy. 

In the debate between modularity and hierarchy, one does not have to take sides. Postle (2006), for example, made a convincing argument that working memory is not localized in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), but is rather an emergent property of widely-distributed brain functioning. While this sounds like an argument for modular independence, Postle’s theory is also compatible with the hierarchical view of brain function; he recognizes the fact that association areas like the PFC do indeed play different roles than primary sensory and motor areas. Specifically, he argues that PFC functions include mediating interference and distraction, maintaining flexible control, preparing responses, and expecting rewards. While others have suggested that the PFC is a substrate for the storage of information in working memory, Postle (2006) maintains that the PFC is composed of coordination modules. In contrast, the capacity-limited functions of working memory (i.e., the so-called phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and episodic buffer) arise from the coordinated activity of broadly distributed brain areas. This relocation of working memory buffers from the PFC to the brain’s representational areas is consistent with Cowan’s (2008) claim that working memory is simply the set of activated / attended content in long-term memory. 

Chein and Schneider (2012) recently sketched out an architecture of neural learning and control that demonstrates the fundamental complementarity of distributed and hierarchical theories of brain function. Their core idea is that the brain is composed of three learning networks: the representation system, the cognitive control system, and the metacognitive network. Their representation system is a modular and distributed set of sensory and motor areas that are--in accordance with Cowan’s (2008) and Postle’s (2006) discussions of working memory--capable of functioning independently of the other two systems. Figures 1 and 2 below demonstrate how these three learning and control systems dynamically interact.

Looking at Figure 2, we see that Chein and Schneider (2012) are postulating three independently functioning and yet highly-coordinated networks. Table 1 below provides some more clarity regarding the biological substrate and evolutionary age of these three brain networks.

Chein and Schneider’s (2012) framework provides an integration point for categorical distinctions, highlighted in the previous section of this paper, regarding the origins of cognition (i.e., whether cognition began in motile bacteria or in animals). It appears that Ginsberg and Jablonka’s *categorizing sensory states* (CSSs) act as prototypes for Chein and Schneider’s metacognitive system. Yet, while Ginsberg and Jablonka (2010) postulated the emergence of CSSs during the Cambrian explosion over 500 million years ago, Chein and Schneider (2012) claim that metacognition emerged in anatomically modern humans, just 150 thousand years ago (see Figure 3 below). Similarly, it appears that Duijn’s (2011) 2 billion year old sensorimotor coordination logic provides the precursor to Chein and Schneider’s 60 million year old cognitive control network. The relation between these objects exemplifies how evolution can reuse organizational frameworks in a variety of ways; this is an illustration of the functionalist term, multiple realizability. In other words, the *functional* *templates* that animal volition systems employ are much older than their current implementation. 

*Figure 3\.* A timeline of evolution on Earth.  
![][image4]  
*Note*: Figure retrieved from [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline\_of\_evolution](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_evolution) on 12/8/12.

As insightful as the Chein and Schneider (2012) framework is, they are probably wrong about a couple things. First, representation (i.e., memory) did not begin with reptiles, some 300 million years ago. Ginsberg and Jablonka (2010) have made a convincing case that associative learning and memory emerged early in metazoan evolution and that it was, perhaps, a major factor in the Cambrian explosion some 550 million years ago. Second, Chein and Schneider (2012) claim that the medial temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus, handles the coordination of episodic memory. While it is partly correct that episodic memory relies on the medial temporal lobe, there is good evidence suggesting that other areas are involved. Schacter, Addis and Buckner (2007) present a cogent argument that episodic memory--the representation of one’s personal experiences--shares the same neural substrates as prospective memory. Figure 4 below illustrates the neural substrates of episodic/prospective memory, which include the medial and lateral temporal lobes as well as parts of the prefrontal, retrosplenial, and parietal lobes. In other words, the “episodic buffer” is more distributed than Chein and Schneider (2012) have claimed. 

*Figure 4\.* Substrates of episodic / prospective memory.  
![][image5]  
*Note:* This figure copied from Schacter, Addis & Buckner (2007).

In summary, the story of modern animal volition requires a number of characters from all over the brain. These characters manifest, or recall, ancient archetypes. Of course, animal volition is a controversial topic but it is perhaps less so than the focus of this paper’s final section: intelligence.

## **5\. INTELLIGENT CREATURES** {#5.-intelligent-creatures}

Episodic/prospective memory (see the grey arrows in Figure 1\) is the defining attribute of intelligence. That is, I agree with Hawkins and Blakeslee’s (2004) memory-prediction framework, which claims that intelligence is a problem-solving method that involves foresight. Intelligence requires prospection--a mode of thinking that involves imagining the future, thinking about the perspectives of others, and/or imagining what is unsensed during navigation. 

At what point did intelligence and prospection emerge on Earth? Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) recount evidence in support of the Bischof-Kohler hypothesis, which states that nonhuman animals are incapable of ﬂexibly entertaining future drive states (i.e., future CSSs); they claim that nonhuman minds are not able to distinguish prospective thoughts from sensations and memories. Humans may be the only creatures equipped with this ability because of our adaptation to the symbolic niche of language and culture (see Deacon, 2007). For example, the fact that nonhuman language users--e.g., lab-trained apes and dolphins--fail to employ linguistic *tenses* may be an indication that humans are the only prospective species. This is the conclusion that Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) have settled upon.

However, there is ample evidence that birds and higher mammals prepare for the future (e.g., by nesting) and imagine the internal states of others (e.g., by stroking victims of aggression). For example, the food-caching behavior of Western scrub jays clearly demonstrates prospective coordination (Emery & Clayton, 2008). Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) counter that these behaviors do not indicate mental time travel, per se, because these animals do not demonstrate to the type of behavioral flexibility that prospection permits. In this regard, Suddendorf and Corballis have put too much stake in prospection. Intelligence does require foresight, but it is a bit naive to claim that the flexibility of human behavior provides a clear criterion for intelligent behavior. Instead, it seems plausible that the evolution of birds--some 150 million years ago, predating the evolution of higher mammals like dolphins and apes--marked the arrival of prospection on Earth.

If not prospective abilities, what distinguishes humans from the rest of Earth’s intelligent creatures? What accounts for our unprecedented dominance and behavioral flexibility? While this is a very important and controversial topic, I will limit the scope of our discussion to ideas presented in Deacon’s (2007) book, *The Symbolic Species.* According to Deacon, the critical event in human evolution was the emergence of abstract symbol networks like language. The ability to represent complex and internally-coherent systems of meaning is exclusively human. These meaning systems consist of abstract entities, abstract properties of such entities, and abstract relationships between them. 

Understanding human languages and cultures requires an understanding of niche construction; humans create niches made of symbols much as beavers create niches made of sticks (Deacon, 2007). Moreover, it is *not* a language acquisition device--innate grammatical ability as proposed by Chomsky (1965)--that enables children to acquire human languages so readily. Instead, this capacity for symbolic reference is made possible by our enlarged prefrontal cortex. Linguistic anthropologists suggest that two million years ago--when humans were a scavenging species, before we became hunter gatherers, during the time of *Homo habilis*\--we began to use language (Bickerton, 2009). While each individual acquired an internal representation of the language, these meaning systems were used as cultural objects, existing outside of individual minds (Deacon, 2007). In turn, the enriched cultural environment (the symbolic *niche*) exerted strong selective pressure for the spectacular brain evolution observed in the homo fossil record. 

Thus, Deacon (2007) concludes, there must be a feedback loop between encephalization and enculturation, leading to the parallel expansion of both. This idea--that evolution coordinates cognitive and morphological habits--also forms the basis of Ginsberg and Jablonka’s (2011) claim that associative learning was a driving force in the Cambrian explosion. More importantly for the purpose of this section, this evolutionary feedback loop explains how and why humans are not merely intelligent creatures; we are also a deeply symbolic species. 

## 

## **6\. CONCLUSION**

Our discussion began with the premise that, by definition, all objects of nature exist because they coordinate the habits of their constituent parts. If nature ceased the coordination of habits, entropy would take over and the universe would be drained of all information. Instead, what we observe in biological evolution is the increase of information in the universe. 

From this starting point, we turned to the categorization of cognition within the biological realm. A distinction was drawn between the sensorimotor and the associative learning criteria. Whereas Duijn’s (2011) sensorimotor criterion includes motile creatures like *E Coli* but excludes sessile creatures like plants, Ginsberg and Jablonka’s (2011) associative learning criterion grants cognition only to cephalized animals. The importance of the brain lies in its communication abilities; the synaptic plasticity of neurons complements the brain’s hierarchical, modular, reentrant network architecture, providing the only known substrate for consciousness, motivation, classical and operant conditioning. 

Sensorimotor control and associative learning are certainly distinct forms of habit coordination (i.e., distinct objects of nature), and this distinction forms the logical basis of Chein and Schneider’s (2012) model. We considered the idea that sensorimotor coordination habits were specialized by the brain’s cognitive control network while habits of categorizing system states (CSSs) were coordinated by the brain’s metacognitive system. Chein and Schneider’s representation network was claimed to be the effective circuitry of working memory. 

Along the way, we began to specify which brain areas support which cognitive functions. The bird and mammal brain’s structural modularity and functional hierarchy was claimed to coordinate “higher-order” habits (e.g., episodic/prospective memory and, by extension, intelligence) that scholars typically reserve for humankind. Abstract / symbolic thought was held up as the only exclusively human cognitive domain. Consciousness, on the other hand, was claimed to be ubiquitous in the animal kingdom. 

In closing, I must admit that this discussion is incomplete. I set out to provide a scientifically palatable explanation for all things cognitive. While this paper should be palatable to its intended readers, I have failed to explain *all things* cognitive. Important topics like conceptual priming, perceptual biases, social cognition and resource limitations have been ignored. At one point, I considered titling this paper “On the Evolution of (Damn-well Nearly) All Things Cognitive” but alas the buzz of self-consciousness disposed me otherwise.
